overview.text: The Kursk Root icon is a particular image of the Mother of God of the Sign, closely associated with ROCOR. The Synod’s history relates its name to its discovery beside a tree root in the Kursk region.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening paragraphs: iconographic type and discovery

blocks.text: The Mother of God appears in prayer with Christ before her; the surrounding figures are Old Testament prophets. The Synod dates the addition of the prophetic surround to 1597, when Tsar Feodor Ioannovich ordered the icon brought to Moscow.

blocks.text: The Synod’s narrative dates the hunter’s discovery to 1295 and relates a spring appearing when he lifts the icon. It also recounts the image’s being cut in two during an attack in 1383 and miraculously reuniting after the priest’s return. These are the source’s received accounts.

blocks.text: The account records its departure from Russia in 1920 and placement in Belgrade in 1925. It identifies the icon with the life of the Russian Church Abroad and notes that Saint John of Shanghai and San Francisco died before it in 1966.
